content: The emergency department (ED), also known as the emergency room (ER), accident and emergency (A&E), or casualty department, is a critical hospital or primary care unit that provides immediate medical care to patients with a wide range of illnesses and injuries, some of which may be life-threatening and require urgent attention. The development of emergency departments in the 20th century was driven by the need for rapid assessment and management of critical conditions. In some countries, EDs serve as essential access points for individuals without other means of obtaining medical care. Upon arrival at the ED, patients typically undergo a brief triage process conducted by a trained nurse to determine the nature and severity of their condition. Those with serious illnesses are prioritized and seen by a physician more quickly than those with less severe symptoms. After initial evaluation and treatment, patients may be admitted to the hospital, stabilized and transferred to another facility, or discharged. The ED staff includes not only physicians but also physician assistants (PAs), nurses with specialized training in emergency medicine, emergency medical technicians (EMTs), respiratory therapists, radiology technicians, healthcare assistants (HCAs), volunteers, and other support personnel. These professionals work collaboratively to provide care to patients and support anxious family members. Most EDs operate 24/7, although staffing levels are often reduced at night. Patients are initially assigned a chief complaint, such as headache, nausea, or loss of consciousness, rather than a formal diagnosis. This remains the primary focus until a diagnosis is made by the attending physician. The layout of a typical ED includes specialized areas for different severities and types of illnesses. The triage area is where patients are initially evaluated by a triage nurse before being directed to the appropriate section of the ED or another hospital department. Patients with life-threatening conditions may bypass triage and be seen directly by a physician. The resuscitation area is a critical section equipped with defibrillators, airway equipment, oxygen, intravenous lines, fluids, emergency drugs, ECG machines, and sometimes limited X-ray facilities. Portable ultrasound devices and non-invasive ventilation (NIV) equipment may also be available. The majors area is designated for stable patients who require bed confinement and further investigation, while the minors area is for patients with less urgent conditions, such as fractures, dislocations, or lacerations requiring suturing. Many EDs now include a dedicated pediatric area with separate waiting spaces and facilities for children, often staffed by play therapists to reduce anxiety and provide distraction during procedures. Obstetric cases are typically referred directly to maternity wards unless other medical conditions require immediate attention. Psychiatric evaluation areas are often staffed by psychiatrists, mental health nurses, and social workers. Some EDs have a fast track system for minor and quickly treatable conditions, staffed by emergency nurse practitioners, PAs, or physicians. This system allows for expedited care for patients who might otherwise face delays due to more critical cases. Hospitals with EDs usually have prominent signage indicating Emergency or Accident and Emergency to guide patients. In some regions, regulations mandate specific wording on these signs to ensure patients in need of critical care are directed to fully equipped facilities. The terminology for emergency departments varies by region. In Australia and New Zealand, it is commonly referred to as the emergency department, while in the UK, Hong Kong, Singapore, and Ireland, it is known as Accident and Emergency (A&E). The term casualty is now considered outdated in many countries. In the United States, the term emergency room (ER) is widely used, although emergency department (ED) is increasingly preferred among medical professionals. Patients arrive at EDs either independently or via ambulance. Ambulance crews notify the hospital in advance if they are transporting a critically ill patient, and treatment may begin en route under the direction of a physician. Upon arrival, these patients are taken directly to the resuscitation area and managed by a specialized team, such as a trauma team for major injuries. Common critical conditions managed in EDs include cardiac arrest, myocardial infarction (heart attack), major trauma, and acute exacerbations of chronic respiratory diseases like asthma and COPD. Cardiac arrest requires immediate basic and advanced life support, while heart attack patients are triaged to the resuscitation area for oxygen, monitoring, early ECG, and medications like aspirin, morphine, and nitroglycerin. Reperfusion therapy, either through thrombolysis or percutaneous transluminal coronary angioplasty (PTCA), is critical for patients with complete coronary artery blockage. Major trauma cases are managed by trauma teams trained in Advanced Trauma Life Support (ATLS) principles. EDs are equipped with specialized diagnostic and therapeutic tools to handle unstable conditions. These include X-ray rooms, CT scanners, ultrasonography equipment, and STAT labs for rapid laboratory testing. Non-invasive ventilation has reduced the need for intubation in severe COPD exacerbations. Emergency physicians are trained to use and manage specialized equipment, such as defibrillators and traction splints, and often collaborate with pre-hospital care providers like EMTs and paramedics. The golden hour is a critical time frame in emergency care, emphasizing the importance of initiating treatment within one hour of an acute event, such as a heart attack or major trauma. Some EDs in smaller hospitals are located near helipads for rapid inter-hospital transfers to trauma centers. Mental health emergencies are also managed in EDs, with patients presenting voluntarily or being brought in by law enforcement for psychiatric evaluation. These patients may be transferred to psychiatric units for further care. EDs are increasingly used for non-emergency care due to overburdened healthcare systems. Patients with minor conditions often seek care in EDs when their primary care providers are unavailable. This trend is particularly common among lower socioeconomic groups and in regions where access to primary care is limited. Resident physicians in emergency medicine training programs provide a significant portion of care in university hospital EDs, supervised by board-certified attending physicians. Academic resources and training programs support the development of expertise in emergency medicine. In summary, emergency departments are complex, high-pressure environments requiring specialized training, equipment, and coordination to provide rapid and effective care for a wide range of medical emergencies.
